clinicalPearls: A rare X-linked primary immunodeficiency with a characteristic, often catastrophic, susceptibility to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
Two genetic subtypes exist: XLP1 from SH2D1A mutations (loss of the SAP protein) and XLP2 from XIAP (BIRC4) mutations (loss of the XIAP protein).

The classic XLP1 phenotype comprises fulminant infectious mononucleosis or EBV-driven haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, dysgammaglobulinaemia, and lymphoma (usually B-cell and often extranodal or ileocaecal).

XIAP deficiency (XLP2) causes recurrent haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and frequently a Crohn-like inflammatory bowel disease, but is not associated with increased lymphoma risk, a key distinction from XLP1.
Presentation is almost always in boys, and disease is frequently unmasked by primary EBV infection, although features can occur without documented EBV.
Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis presents with prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, hyperferritinaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia and coagulopathy, and is a medical emergency.
Diagnosis combines genetic testing with flow cytometry for absent SAP or XIAP protein expression; absent invariant natural killer T (NKT) cells support XLP1.

Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is the only curative treatment, while immunoglobulin replacement and prompt therapy directed at haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis are important supportive measures.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome results from mutations on the X chromosome that impair immune regulation. In XLP1, mutations in SH2D1A at Xq25 abolish or impair SAP (SLAM-associated protein), a small SH2-domain adaptor that couples the SLAM family of receptors to downstream signalling through Fyn kinase in T cells, natural killer (NK) cells and NKT cells. Loss of SAP impairs cytotoxic T-cell and NK-cell killing of EBV-infected B cells, blocks development of invariant NKT cells, and disrupts T-follicular-helper-cell function and germinal-centre antibody responses, explaining the uncontrolled EBV-driven lymphoproliferation, defective humoral immunity and lymphoma predisposition. In XLP2, mutations in XIAP (BIRC4, also at Xq25) cause loss of the X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis protein, which normally restrains excessive programmed cell death and modulates inflammatory signalling through the NOD2/NF-kB pathway and the inflammasome; its loss leads to lymphocyte hypersensitivity to apoptosis, defective control of EBV, recurrent haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and Crohn-like inflammatory bowel disease, but not the lymphoma risk seen in XLP1. In both subtypes, failure to contain EBV can precipitate a hyperinflammatory, macrophage-activating haemophagocytic syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Familial (primary) haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (PRF1, UNC13D/Munc13-4, STX11, STXBP2)
Other EBV-susceptibility immunodeficiencies, such as MAGT1 (XMEN), CD27, CD70, ITK, CTPS1 and RASGRP1 deficiencies
Chediak-Higashi syndrome and Griscelli syndrome type 2 (pigmentary dilution with haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis)
Common variable immunodeficiency and other causes of hypogammaglobulinaemia
B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma from other causes
Severe or atypical infectious mononucleosis in an immunocompetent host
For XLP2, monogenic very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing of SH2D1A and XIAP (BIRC4)
Flow cytometry for intracellular SAP and XIAP protein expression
EBV serology and quantitative EBV viral load in blood
Enumeration of invariant NKT cells (absent in XLP1) and NK/T-cell cytotoxicity assays
Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody/vaccine-response studies

Work-up for haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis: full blood count, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, liver function, soluble interleukin-2 receptor and bone-marrow examination for haemophagocytosis
Imaging and tissue biopsy where lymphoma or focal organ involvement is suspected
redFlags: Fulminant or unusually severe infectious mononucleosis, especially in a boy with a suggestive family history
Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (persistent fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, very high ferritin, coagulopathy), which is life-threatening
New lymphadenopathy or an abdominal mass suggesting lymphoma
A maternal family history of males dying of EBV infection, haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or lymphoma
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease, particularly EBV-triggered haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, historically carried a very high mortality. Outcomes have improved markedly with early recognition, therapy directed at haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and curative allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, though the prognosis remains guarded once severe haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or lymphoma is established.
pitfalls: Dismissing severe infectious mononucleosis in a young boy as ordinary EBV infection and missing the underlying immunodeficiency.
Assuming that a normal EBV viral load or EBV-negative status excludes the diagnosis, as disease can occur without documented EBV.
Overlooking XIAP deficiency in boys presenting with recurrent haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or early-onset inflammatory bowel disease.
Delaying assessment for definitive stem-cell transplantation while repeatedly treating recurrent episodes.
Not screening at-risk male relatives and female carriers within the family.
references: Primary immunodeficiency reference texts and the IUIS classification of inborn errors of immunity
